threads.question: Can scientific literature be made genuinely navigable — not just searchable?
threads.take: A ranked list answers one question: which documents match these keywords. It says nothing about how a field is shaped, which results build on which, where two communities are quietly disagreeing, or which corner nobody has looked at yet. The work at SciX has been about putting that structure on top of the ADS corpus, using embeddings for meaning, citation graphs for how the ideas connect, and controlled vocabularies to keep the grounding honest. What sits below is the current state of that, and the papers I read to push on it.

reading_order.why: Start with citation-informed document embeddings: how papers cite each other turns out to teach a model what they mean.
Then the case for domain adaptation: generic models leave signal on the table in specialized corpora.
astroBERT applies that to astronomy, a domain model trained on the same ADS corpus I work in.
Our SciX experiments: embeddings + vector search over the live literature, and what broke.
Close on knowledge graphs, the structural layer ranked retrieval can never give you.

threads.question: What makes multi-agent systems reliable enough to change real production code?
threads.take: Most agent demos work once. Production is the opposite problem: the same task run a thousand times, with no one watching the single run that quietly corrupts a repository. The work at Sourcegraph lives underneath that, in orchestration, verification, and blast-radius control rather than in cleverer prompts. Below is what I'm building toward reliability, sitting next to the empirical work on where agents actually break.

reading_order.why: Vocabulary first: the architectural patterns agents are built from.
A concrete open platform for agents that act on real codebases.
The survey view across the software-engineering lifecycle.
Then the failure modes: an empirical dissection of where agentic frameworks break.
And a production deployment, where reliability stops being academic.

threads.question: How should agents remember across long horizons?
threads.take: An agent with no memory re-derives the world every turn; an agent that remembers the wrong things compounds its own mistakes instead. Most of the open work sits between those two failures: what to store, when to consolidate, and what to let the system forget. I mapped that literature into an explorer of 108 papers across nine themes and a five-part podcast, so the ideas stay learnable rather than only citable. The papers below are two recent threads I'm still pulling on.

reading_order.why: Memory as built from the agent's own experience, via contrastive reflection.
Memory as a graph of tools, optimized jointly with the policy.

threads.question: How do we evaluate coding agents honestly, at scale?
threads.take: A benchmark that looks impressive and measures nothing is worse than no benchmark, because now the number carries authority it never earned. Most coding-agent evaluations still test toy tasks, report one pass rate, and get cited as if they settled the question. The benchmarks I build target large, real software changes, and the writing next to them is mostly a long argument with the popular ones. Below is that work and the reading that keeps me honest about what good is supposed to mean.

reading_order.why: The lay of the land: how code-generation models are surveyed and measured.
Calibration: whether the models know when they are right, an honesty signal most benchmarks ignore.
What goes into training shapes what the benchmark sees: data quality for code generators.
Moving past static pass@k toward outcome-based RL signals.
